extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in Apple, technology, and journalism/editorial practices
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the editorial standards and practices Apple uses to select and feature top stories in the Apple News app, emphasizing human judgment over algorithmic selection. Explains selection of both stories and sources, vetting for trustworthiness, balancing viewpoints, and handling sensitive topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human curation (people, not algorithms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple uses people — a small editorial team — rather than algorithms to pick its top stories for the Apple News app.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apple believes humans can better follow the news cycle and judge what’s important: “We’re so much more subtly following the news cycle and what’s important,” and that human judgment is currently “the only legitimate way to do it at this point.” Human curation is presented as a way to avoid algorithmic prejudice that can be baked into code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top-five featured stories
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial team selects the five stories to feature at the top of the app at any one time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The team meets (e.g., huddles each morning) to agree on the day’s top news and to decide which five items should be featured. Selection involves reading through multiple versions and choosing the best rendition and source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose sources that provide context and explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple outlets cover the same event, editors choose the story (and source) that provides the most context and explanation of why the news matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when several sites led with a DOJ/Harvard affirmative-action story, editors selected The Washington Post’s report because it provided the most context and explanation. The process involves comparing versions and picking the one that best explains significance to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vetting for trustworthiness (the 'smell test')
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors will not run stories they do not trust or that fail informal credibility checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Apple News did not run an ABC News story about Michael Flynn because the editors “didn’t trust it” and it didn’t “pass the smell test.” This vetting relies on human judgment rather than algorithmic formulas for verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide views from both sides of political debates
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple News strives to offer readers viewpoints from across the political spectrum rather than favoring one side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When launching an elections section Apple highlighted partners from differing perspectives (e.g., Fox News and Vox) and noted there are substantial readers of both traditionally left-leaning and right-leaning publications on the platform. The editorial aim is balance in featured coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible coverage of sensitive topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors consider how sensitive stories should be reported and which report to feature to ensure responsible coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for racially charged remarks in a Florida governor race, editors selected a nuanced Miami Herald piece that examined comments, context, and the debate, reflecting deliberate choice of a careful, contextualized treatment for sensitive subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility to maintain sanity and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial team accepts responsibility for what appears in Apple News and aims to prevent the feed from becoming unreliable or chaotic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roger Rosner: “We are responsible for what’s in there… We’re not just going to let it be a total crazy land.” Human curation is framed as key to preserving sanity and reliability in the app’s news selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about algorithmic bias
rubrics_metrics.description: A stated reason for human curation is concern that algorithms can encode bias (e.g., labeling outlets as liberal or conservative) and thus reproduce prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ms. Kern criticized the view that algorithms alone avoid prejudice, arguing that bias can be baked into algorithmic code; human editors are presented as better positioned to mitigate such encoded biases.
